content.title: About
content.content: Swiss cheese is a semi‑hard cheese with characteristic holes, made from cow’s milk. It has a mild nutty flavor and a slightly sweet aroma. Traditional aging ranges from 3 to 12 months, during which the iconic “eyes” develop.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Swiss cheese is best known under the brand name “Emmental,” though Switzerland produces many regional varieties.
The holes are created by Propionibacterium freudenreichii bacteria, which release carbon dioxide.
It is a key ingredient in fondue, a classic Swiss melted‑cheese dish.
In the United States the cheese is simply called “Swiss cheese,” while in Switzerland it has different regional names.
When aged up to 24 months, the flavor becomes more intense and aromatic.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium supports strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Protein is essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, which aid nerve function and metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic bacteria
items.content: The bacteria used in ripening may benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: Low in lactose
items.content: During aging much of the lactose is broken down, making it more tolerable for people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may react to Swiss cheese.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The cheese is salty, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of its fat content, it is calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Excess saturated fat may raise cholesterol levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Swiss cheese is great sliced for sandwiches, added to salads, grated over pasta and casseroles, melted in fondue, baked in gratins, or used as a filling for omelets.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cheese in the refrigerator wrapped in wax paper or parchment, then placed in a plastic container. Properly stored, it keeps its flavor for 4‑6 weeks. Discard if any non‑white mold appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Ham luncheon meat, loaf type (item 1009) is a cooked meat product made from selected cuts of pork, beef and sometimes chicken breast, finely ground, formed into a solid loaf shape and baked. It has a pink hue, a tender texture and a mild smoky aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Loaf‑type ham first appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient way to store meat for long periods.
A fine emulsion process is used to achieve a uniform texture, grinding the meat into a paste and mixing it with water, salt and spices.
The loaf is often sliced thinly for sandwiches, salads and snack platters.
It can be stored for up to 12 months at 0 °C to +4 °C without quality loss.
Loaf‑type ham is a staple in military rations and expedition meals because of its shelf stability.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Contains about 15–18 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Iron contributes to hemoglobin formation and energy metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Supplies vitamins B1, B3, B6 and B12, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Practically carbohydrate‑free, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Convenient and portable
items.content: Ready‑to‑eat product that requires no cooking.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The product is often salty; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Nitrites and other preservatives may be used for shelf life; excessive consumption can be undesirable.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork or beef.

items.title: Heat treatment
items.content: Although ready to eat, heating can be done; overheating may produce an off‑flavor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ham can be eaten straight from the package, sliced thin for sandwiches, added to salads, omelets or hot dishes. It pairs well with mustard, cheese, pickles and bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0 °C to +4 °C. After opening, consume within 5–7 days. For long‑term storage (up to 12 months) keep the sealed original package in a cool place.

ham-or-pork-with-tomato-based-sauce.title: Ham or Pork with Tomato-Based Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Ham or pork pieces cooked in a flavorful tomato-based sauce are a ready‑to‑eat meat product. The sauce adds a gentle tang and rich taste, while the meat stays tender and juicy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauce often includes basil, oregano, and garlic, making it a staple of Mediterranean cuisine.
Tomatoes used in the sauce are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Ham can be smoked or boiled; this product typically uses boiled ham for a milder flavor.
The product can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 5 days after opening.
Tomato sauce is a common base for pasta, pizza, and stews.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Pork contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Lycopene in tomatoes
items.content: Lycopene has antioxidant properties and supports heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the meat and the sauce supply B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: The product is suitable for low‑carb diets as it contains virtually no sugar.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ham is often salty; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some versions may contain nitrites, which are undesirable in large amounts.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, an allergy to pork can occur.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: The product contains saturated fats; moderate consumption is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat: heat it in the microwave or on a skillet, add it to pasta, rice, vegetable stews, or use it as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in the original packaging. After opening, consume within 5‑7 days. When frozen, quality is maintained for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta is a product made from wheat flour and water (sometimes eggs) that is shaped and then boiled in salted water until tender. Cooked pasta serves as a base for countless dishes, from simple sauces to elaborate casseroles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The earliest references to pasta date back to ancient Rome, but its modern form was refined in Italy during the Middle Ages.
There are more than 600 shapes of pasta, each designed to pair best with specific sauces.
Traditional Italian pasta is made from durum wheat, a hard wheat that gives it a firm structure and helps it hold its shape during cooking.
In Japan, soba (buckwheat noodles) is popular, while rice noodles dominate Chinese cuisine.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides a steady release of energy, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B3 support carbohydrate metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for blood formation and normal muscle function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Cooked pasta contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: It can be combined with vegetables, legumes, seafood, or lean meats to create a balanced meal.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Pasta contains gluten, so people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose gluten‑free alternatives.

items.title: Undercooking
items.content: Undercooked pasta can be hard to digest and cause gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Boiling water is often heavily salted; excessive sodium intake may raise blood pressure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook pasta in salted water until al dente, then drain. Serve it with tomato, cream, pesto sauces, add it to soups, casseroles, or salads. For a lighter option, choose whole‑grain or legume‑based pasta.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry pasta in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked pasta, cooled to room temperature, should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 3‑4 days in a sealed container.

content.title: About
content.content: Pinto beans are dried beans that have been lightly enriched with added fat to improve flavor and texture. They have a light brown color with speckles, a mild nutty aroma, and a soft, slightly creamy consistency when cooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pinto beans originated in Mexico and are a staple in Latin American cuisine.
Dried pinto beans are commonly used in chili, soups, stews, and salads.
Adding a small amount of fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Pinto is one of the most popular bean varieties in the United States.
When stored properly, dried beans can last up to a year.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: A 100 g serving of dry beans provides about 21 g of protein, making them an excellent source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are important for blood formation and anemia prevention.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps stabilize blood sugar levels, beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: The added fat is usually a plant oil, supplying energy and aiding the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking beans before cooking helps mitigate this.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive people; proper soaking and cooking reduce the effect.

items.title: Sodium in processed product
items.content: If the beans are fat‑enriched, salt is sometimes added; monitor sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Soak pinto beans in water for at least 6–8 hours, then boil until tender (about 1–1.5 hours). Cooked beans can be added to chili, soups, salads, purees, or used in vegetarian patties. For extra flavor, lightly sauté the beans with vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried pinto beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Properly stored, they remain good for up to 12 months. After opening, keep moisture out to prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Popsicle is a popular brand of frozen lollies produced by NFS. The product is a frozen fruit or cream‑based dessert on a stick, coated with a sweet glaze and often colored and flavored with vibrant additives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Popsicle was created in 1905 when 11‑year‑old Fred Herring accidentally froze juice on a wooden stick.
The name "Popsicle" became a generic term for any ice pop in the United States.
NFS offers more than 30 flavors, ranging from classic fruit and berry to inventive combos like mango‑chili.
Each serving contains about 70 kcal, making it a popular low‑calorie snack.
Popsicles are frequently used in culinary shows as a base for creative desserts and cocktails.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Because it is mostly water and frozen juice, a Popsicle provides very few calories.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fruit varieties supply vitamin C and potassium, supporting immune function and fluid balance.

items.title: Refreshing effect
items.content: The cold treat quickly cools you down on hot days and helps quench thirst.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Most flavors contain added sugar, which may be undesirable for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some versions may contain dairy, nuts, or food colorings that can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Cold shock
items.content: Eating directly from the freezer can cause tooth or throat discomfort in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Popsicles are eaten straight from the wrapper, holding the stick. They make a convenient refreshing snack for children, can be added to cocktails, or sliced to garnish desserts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Popsicles in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once removed from the packaging, they should be consumed within 24 hours to prevent ice crystal formation and flavor loss.
